Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN)  -- The United States and Britain said Wednesday they are committed to remaining in Afghanistan, despite increased military casualties and declining public support for the war effort. U.S. Marines partrol part of the Gharmsir district in Afghanistan's Helmand province on Wednesday. "We went into this together, and we will work it through together because we are stronger together," British Foreign Secretary David Miliband said after a half day of talks at the State Department with Secretary of State Hillary Clinton. Clinton praised Miliband's approach on Afghanistan, including the call for the government to reconcile with moderate elements of the Taliban. "His analysis of the way forward is very much consistent with ours, and we will continue to stand shoulder to shoulder in pursuit of our common objectives," Clinton said of her counterpart. In a speech at NATO headquarters on Monday, Miliband called for rank-and-file Taliban to be given the chance to reconcile with the Afghan government, even as the campaign continues against Taliban commanders who are waging jihad. He also urged greater burden sharing not only among NATO allies in Afghanistan but by the Afghan government. "There is a lot of talk, rightly, about burden sharing within the coalition, but the greatest burden sharing must be between the international community and the government of Afghanistan, which increasingly needs to take the lead -- the security lead, as well as the political lead -- in shaping the future of that country," he said. Richard Holbrooke, the U.S. special representative for Afghanistan and Pakistan, told reporters that boosting the training of Afghan forces would be a big focus after the country's August 20 election. When asked whether the election would be fair, Holbrooke, who just returned from the region, said he had heard complaints from all sides but was not "unduly upset." "It's an extraordinary thing to hold an election in the middle of a war, and this is the first contested election in Afghanistan in history," Holbrooke said, adding the United States has no favorite candidate but only wants "an election whose outcome is accepted as legitimate by the Afghan people and the world, which reflects the desires of those who vote." July has been the deadliest month for U.S. and British forces since the U.S.-led invasion in 2001, with 39 U.S. troops and 22 British troops killed. Miliband said the effort was going through a "tough phase," but added that the British people understood the "vital nature" of the mission to stabilize Afghanistan. British Prime Minister Gordon Brown has been under under enormous pressure from his opposition, which charges that British troops don't have proper resources to fight the war, including helicopters. But he was sanguine. "I think the British people will stay with this mission, because there is a clear strategy and a clear determination on behalf of the United States and other coalition members to see this through," he said, adding that the British people understood the mission's "vital nature." Americans, too, have questioned whether the war in Afghanistan is winnable and worth the effort. U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates and members of Congress, including Democrats, have predicted that President Obama has a year to show progress in Afghanistan before public support for the war further erodes. Clinton said Britain and the United States "have made significant gains in the recent operations" against the Taliban, but "there remains much work to be done." "We know that this is a challenge that is not going to be easily resolved in a short period of time," she said, adding "both of our countries are still threatened by the same enemy, an enemy that has attacked London, New York and Washington." "We know they've attacked us in the past, and, unfortunately, we know that they plot against us even today," she said.

WASHINGTON (CNN) — The United States and Britain said Wednesday that they remain committed to their mission in Afghanistan despite mounting military casualties and declining public support for the war effort.

U.S. Marines patrolled part of the Gharmsir district in Afghanistan’s Helmand province on Wednesday.

“We went into this together, and we will work it through together because we are stronger together,” British Foreign Secretary David Miliband said after a half-day of talks with Secretary of State Hillary Clinton at the State Department.

Clinton praised Miliband’s approach to Afghanistan, including his call for the government to pursue reconciliation with moderate elements of the Taliban.

“His analysis of the way forward is very much consistent with ours, and we will continue to stand shoulder to shoulder in pursuit of our common objectives,” Clinton said of her counterpart.

In a speech at NATO headquarters on Monday, Miliband called for rank-and-file Taliban members to be given an opportunity to reconcile with the Afghan government, even as the campaign continues against Taliban commanders waging jihad.

He also urged greater burden-sharing—not only among NATO allies in Afghanistan, but also by the Afghan government.

“There is a lot of talk, rightly, about burden sharing within the coalition, but the greatest burden sharing must be between the international community and the government of Afghanistan, which increasingly needs to take the lead—the security lead, as well as the political lead—in shaping the future of that country,” he said.

Richard Holbrooke, the U.S. special representative for Afghanistan and Pakistan, told reporters that expanding the training of Afghan forces would be a major focus following the country’s August 20 election.

Asked whether the election would be fair, Holbrooke, who had just returned from the region, said he had heard complaints from all sides but was not “unduly upset.”

“It’s an extraordinary thing to hold an election in the middle of a war, and this is the first contested election in Afghanistan in history,” Holbrooke said. He added that the United States had no preferred candidate and sought only “an election whose outcome is accepted as legitimate by the Afghan people and the world, which reflects the desires of those who vote.”

July has been the deadliest month for U.S. and British forces since the U.S.-led invasion in 2001, with 39 U.S. troops and 22 British troops killed.

Miliband said the effort was going through a “tough phase,” but added that the British people understood the “vital nature” of the mission to stabilize Afghanistan.

British Prime Minister Gordon Brown has faced enormous pressure from the opposition, which contends that British troops lack the resources needed to fight the war, including helicopters. Nevertheless, he remained sanguine.

“I think the British people will stay with this mission, because there is a clear strategy and a clear determination on behalf of the United States and other coalition members to see this through,” he said, adding that the British people understood the mission’s “vital nature.”

Americans, too, have questioned whether the war in Afghanistan is winnable and worth the effort. U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates and members of Congress, including Democrats, have predicted that President Obama has one year to demonstrate progress in Afghanistan before public support for the war erodes further.

Clinton said Britain and the United States “have made significant gains in the recent operations” against the Taliban, but acknowledged that “there remains much work to be done.”

“We know that this is a challenge that is not going to be easily resolved in a short period of time,” she said, adding that “both of our countries are still threatened by the same enemy, an enemy that has attacked London, New York and Washington.”

“We know they’ve attacked us in the past, and, unfortunately, we know that they plot against us even today,” she said.

WASHINGTON (CNN) — The United States and the United Kingdom reaffirmed Wednesday that they would continue their involvement in Afghanistan, even as military deaths rise and public backing for the conflict weakens.

On Wednesday, U.S. Marines were patrolling an area of Gharmsir district in Afghanistan’s Helmand province.

Following several hours of discussions with Secretary of State Hillary Clinton at the State Department, British Foreign Secretary David Miliband emphasized the unity between the two countries.

The nations entered the conflict jointly and would see it through as partners, he said, arguing that cooperation made them stronger.

Clinton welcomed Miliband’s strategy for Afghanistan, particularly his proposal that the Afghan government seek reconciliation with moderate members of the Taliban. She said his assessment of the path ahead closely matched the U.S. position and pledged that Washington and London would remain united in working toward their shared goals.

During an address at NATO headquarters Monday, Miliband argued that ordinary Taliban members should be offered an opportunity to make peace with the Afghan government. At the same time, he said military operations should continue against Taliban leaders conducting jihad.

Miliband also called for a fairer distribution of responsibilities, both among NATO countries operating in Afghanistan and between the international coalition and the Afghan government. Although burden sharing within the coalition was an important subject, he said, the most significant transfer of responsibility should occur between the international community and Afghanistan’s government. Afghan authorities, he added, must increasingly assume control of both security and political decision-making as the country determines its future.

Richard Holbrooke, the U.S. special representative for Afghanistan and Pakistan, told journalists that expanding the training of Afghan security forces would become a major priority following Afghanistan’s August 20 election.

Asked whether the vote would be conducted fairly, Holbrooke—who had recently returned from the region—said he had heard grievances from every side but was not excessively concerned. Holding an election during a war was remarkable, he said, noting that it would be the first competitive election in Afghan history.

Holbrooke also said the United States did not support any particular candidate. Washington’s objective, he explained, was an election whose result would be viewed as legitimate by Afghans and the international community and would accurately represent the wishes of those who cast ballots.

July was the most lethal month for American and British forces since the U.S.-led invasion began in 2001. During the month, 39 U.S. service members and 22 British troops were killed.

Miliband acknowledged that the mission was experiencing a difficult period, but said the British public recognized how essential it was to stabilize Afghanistan.

British Prime Minister Gordon Brown had faced intense criticism from opposition politicians, who claimed British forces lacked the equipment necessary for the conflict, including helicopters. Nevertheless, Brown remained confident. He said the public would continue supporting the mission because the United States and other coalition partners had a clearly defined strategy and were determined to complete it. He also said Britons understood the mission’s crucial importance.

In the United States, people had likewise raised doubts about whether victory in Afghanistan was possible and whether the campaign justified its costs. Defense Secretary Robert Gates and several members of Congress, including Democrats, had predicted that President Obama had one year to demonstrate progress before public support declined further.

Clinton said recent operations against the Taliban had produced substantial advances for Britain and the United States, while cautioning that much remained to be accomplished. She stressed that the situation could not be resolved quickly or easily.

Both countries, Clinton added, continued to face the same adversary—one that had carried out attacks in London, New York and Washington. That enemy had struck before and, she warned, was still planning attacks against them.

The United States and Britain reaffirmed their commitment to the mission in Afghanistan despite mounting military casualties and weakening public support for the war. Officials from both countries stressed that they would continue working together to address the security and political challenges facing Afghanistan.

British Foreign Secretary David Miliband advocated a strategy that would combine sustained military pressure with efforts to reconcile with moderate, rank-and-file members of the Taliban. He argued that insurgents who were willing to renounce violence and participate in Afghanistan’s political process should be offered a path toward reintegration. At the same time, military operations should continue against senior Taliban commanders and others committed to the insurgency.

U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton said Miliband’s proposals closely reflected the American approach. She emphasized that Washington and London remained aligned on Afghanistan and would continue coordinating their military, diplomatic, and development efforts.

Miliband also called for greater burden sharing, particularly by transferring more responsibility to the Afghan government. He said Afghan authorities needed to take a stronger role in providing security and demonstrating effective political leadership.

U.S. special envoy Richard Holbrooke similarly identified the training of Afghan security forces as a major priority following the August 20 election. Addressing complaints surrounding the vote, Holbrooke indicated that he was not overly concerned, suggesting that disputes and allegations were not unexpected in Afghanistan’s developing democratic system.

The United States and Britain reaffirmed their commitment to the mission in Afghanistan despite mounting military casualties, the conflict’s growing financial cost, and declining public support in both countries. Leaders acknowledged the seriousness of these concerns but argued that withdrawing before Afghan institutions were capable of maintaining security would risk allowing the country once again to become a refuge for extremist organizations.

Their approach combines military pressure with a broader political strategy. While coalition forces will continue operations against Taliban commanders and other militant leaders who remain committed to violence, the two governments support reconciliation with members of the Taliban who are prepared to renounce terrorism, lay down their weapons, and participate peacefully in Afghanistan’s constitutional political process. Such outreach is intended to divide reconcilable fighters from hard-line leaders and reduce the insurgency’s local support.

Washington and London also called for greater burden sharing among NATO members and other international partners. They stressed that success requires more than additional combat forces: countries can contribute trainers, civilian experts, development assistance, equipment, and support for Afghan institutions. A coordinated international effort is necessary to improve governance, combat corruption, encourage economic development, and provide Afghans with credible alternatives to insurgent influence.

A central element of the strategy is the accelerated training and expansion of Afghanistan’s army and police. Stronger, better-led Afghan security forces are expected gradually to assume responsibility for protecting the population and conducting operations, allowing foreign troops to move into supporting roles over time. The goal is not an indefinite international military presence, but a phased transition based on Afghan capacity and conditions on the ground.

Ultimately, the shared American-British strategy places Afghan ownership at the center of the mission. Political authority, security responsibility, and decisions about reconciliation must increasingly rest with the Afghan government and its people. International partners will continue to provide assistance and pressure militant networks, but lasting stability will depend on effective Afghan leadership, accountable institutions, and sustained cooperation among Afghanistan’s allies.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about U.S. and British officials reaffirming their commitment to the war in Afghanistan despite rising casualties and weakening public support.
counterfactuals.output:
# U.S., British officials reaffirm Afghanistan mission amid rising casualties

**WASHINGTON/LONDON** — U.S. and British officials are reaffirming their commitment to the war in Afghanistan, insisting that the mission remains vital to national security despite mounting troop deaths and declining public support on both sides of the Atlantic.

Officials said the campaign is aimed at preventing Afghanistan from again becoming a haven for al Qaeda and other militant groups. They acknowledged growing frustration with the conflict but warned that withdrawing before Afghan forces can secure the country could reverse hard-won gains.

The renewed pledges come as coalition casualties rise and military commanders confront a resilient Taliban insurgency, particularly in southern and eastern Afghanistan. British forces have faced intense fighting in Helmand province, while U.S. troops have expanded operations in several contested regions.

Public opinion surveys in both countries have shown increasing skepticism about the war’s direction, with many voters questioning its cost, objectives and prospects for success. The conflict has also come under pressure from lawmakers demanding clearer benchmarks and a credible timetable for transferring security responsibilities to Afghan forces.

U.S. officials have emphasized that military operations must be accompanied by efforts to improve governance, reduce corruption and expand economic development. British leaders have made similar arguments, saying success cannot be measured solely by territory captured or insurgents killed.

The strategy depends heavily on strengthening Afghanistan’s army and police so international forces can eventually take a reduced role. But training efforts have been complicated by desertions, limited resources and concerns about the effectiveness of Afghan institutions.

NATO allies are also under pressure to provide additional troops, equipment and civilian assistance. Some coalition members have placed restrictions on where their forces can operate, creating tension within the alliance over how the burden of the war is shared.

Despite those challenges, U.S. and British officials maintain that abandoning the mission would carry greater risks than continuing it.

Military leaders have cautioned that progress is likely to be slow and that further casualties should be expected. For governments in Washington and London, the challenge is now not only defeating insurgent networks but also persuading increasingly doubtful publics that the war remains necessary — and winnable.

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on Hillary Clinton and David Miliband’s State Department talks concerning Afghanistan, including Taliban reconciliation, NATO burden sharing, Afghan force training, and the August 20 election.
counterfactuals.output:
### Clinton–Miliband talks on Afghanistan

At a joint appearance at the State Department in Washington on **July 29, 2009**, Secretary of State **Hillary Clinton** and British Foreign Secretary **David Miliband** emphasized a common U.S.–British strategy in Afghanistan ahead of the August presidential election.

- **Taliban reconciliation:** Both supported an Afghan-led effort to reintegrate insurgents who were fighting for money, fear, or local grievances rather than ideological commitment. Clinton said reconciliation was possible only for those willing to **renounce violence, break with al-Qaeda, and accept Afghanistan’s constitution and political system**. Neither advocated negotiations with irreconcilable Taliban or al-Qaeda leaders.

- **NATO burden sharing:** Clinton praised Britain’s major military contribution and losses, particularly in Helmand Province. The two argued that Afghanistan was not solely an American or British war and that NATO members needed to contribute according to their capabilities—including troops, trainers, development assistance, and civilian specialists. Miliband acknowledged domestic concern over casualties but maintained that the mission was tied to international security.

- **Training Afghan forces:** They agreed that long-term success depended on building an Afghan army and police force capable of assuming responsibility for security. More trainers, mentoring teams, equipment, and institutional support were presented as essential to reducing reliance on foreign combat troops. Miliband stressed that military operations had to be combined with effective Afghan governance and economic development.

- **August 20 election:** Clinton and Miliband described the presidential and provincial elections as a critical test. They did not endorse a candidate, instead calling for an **Afghan-run, credible, inclusive, and secure vote**. They acknowledged that insurgent violence and intimidation could prevent perfect conditions, but said legitimacy would depend on broad participation, acceptable procedures, and respect for the results.

Overall, the talks did not unveil a major new initiative. They reinforced a strategy combining military pressure, expansion of Afghan security forces, selective reconciliation, stronger allied participation, and support for a legitimate Afghan political process.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a detailed Washington-dateline news story explaining why the United States and Britain intend to remain in Afghanistan after the deadliest month for their troops since the 2001 invasion.
counterfactuals.output:
**WASHINGTON —** The United States and Britain say they will keep their forces in Afghanistan despite suffering their heaviest monthly losses since the war began in 2001, arguing that a withdrawal now would allow the Taliban to recover, give al-Qaeda renewed sanctuary and threaten the stability of neighboring Pakistan.

July 2009 was the deadliest month of the nearly eight-year conflict for both American and British troops. More than 40 U.S. service members and more than 20 British personnel were killed, according to military casualty tallies, as Western forces launched major operations in Taliban strongholds ahead of Afghanistan’s Aug. 20 presidential election.

The rising toll has intensified political pressure on President Barack Obama and British Prime Minister Gordon Brown. Public support for the war has weakened in both countries, and lawmakers are asking whether the mission has clear, achievable objectives.

Officials in Washington and London, however, contend that the surge in casualties reflects an expansion of military operations rather than evidence that the strategy has failed. Thousands of additional U.S. Marines and British soldiers moved into areas of southern Afghanistan that had long been controlled or heavily influenced by the Taliban. Commanders had warned that losses were likely to rise as troops left heavily defended bases, entered insurgent-held territory and encountered roadside bombs.

The central argument for staying is the same one that took U.S. and British forces into Afghanistan after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks: preventing the country from again becoming a base for international terrorism.

Al-Qaeda’s senior leadership is believed to have shifted across the border into Pakistan, but Western officials say an unchecked Taliban resurgence in Afghanistan could once again give the organization territory in which to train recruits, plan attacks and operate with relative freedom. The Taliban government sheltered Osama bin Laden before the 2001 invasion and refused to hand him over after the attacks on New York and Washington.

Obama has described the fight against al-Qaeda and its allies as a war of necessity, distinguishing it from the conflict in Iraq, which he opposed. His administration’s revised strategy is intended to narrow the mission around disrupting terrorist networks, reversing Taliban gains and building Afghan security forces capable of taking over the fighting.

Another major concern is Pakistan. Afghanistan’s insurgency straddles a border that is mountainous, lightly governed and difficult to police. Taliban and al-Qaeda fighters have used sanctuaries in Pakistan’s tribal regions to recruit, train and launch operations into Afghanistan.

U.S. officials fear that abandoning Afghanistan could strengthen Islamist militants on both sides of the border and place greater pressure on Pakistan, a nuclear-armed country facing its own insurgency. In Washington’s view, the two conflicts are inseparable: success in one country is unlikely if militants can operate freely in the other.

The immediate military objective is to secure population centers in southern and eastern Afghanistan, particularly in Helmand and Kandahar provinces, where the Taliban has maintained a strong presence and where much of the country’s opium is produced.

In Helmand, U.S. Marines launched a large offensive in early July while British troops conducted Operation Panther’s Claw. The aim was not simply to kill insurgents but to clear Taliban-controlled districts, protect civilians, restore government authority and make it possible for Afghans to vote.

That approach reflects the counterinsurgency strategy promoted by Gen. Stanley McChrystal, the newly appointed commander of U.S. and NATO forces in Afghanistan. It places greater emphasis on shielding civilians, limiting airstrikes that could cause civilian casualties and keeping troops in areas after they have been cleared.

Western commanders say earlier operations often drove Taliban fighters out temporarily but failed to provide lasting security. Insurgents returned after foreign and Afghan troops departed, intimidating residents and re-establishing shadow governments.

The strategy therefore requires more troops and exposes them to greater danger. Roadside bombs, or improvised explosive devices, account for a growing share of coalition deaths. Taliban fighters generally avoid prolonged direct battles with better-armed Western units, relying instead on explosives, ambushes and attacks from populated areas.

Officials also argue that withdrawing because of rising casualties would reward that strategy. If insurgents believe they can force Western governments out by inflicting enough losses, military planners say, they will have little incentive to negotiate or abandon the fight.

Britain’s role is particularly important in Helmand, where its forces have been concentrated since 2006. Brown has faced criticism over whether British troops have been given enough helicopters, armored vehicles and other equipment to protect them from bombs. The government insists that commanders’ essential requests are being met, although ministers have acknowledged the need to improve protection and mobility.

Brown has said British forces are in Afghanistan to reduce the threat of terrorism at home, not to impose a Western political system or occupy the country indefinitely. British officials maintain that attacks planned or inspired from the Afghanistan-Pakistan region could eventually reach British streets.

The United States and Britain also say they must protect the limited gains made since the Taliban was driven from power. Millions of Afghan children, including girls who were largely excluded from school under Taliban rule, have entered classrooms. Roads, clinics and government institutions have been built, although progress is uneven and corruption remains widespread.

A rapid Western departure, officials warn, could endanger Afghans who have worked with the central government or foreign forces. It could also undermine women’s rights and other social advances, especially in rural areas where the Taliban remains influential.

Yet neither Washington nor London publicly describes the goal as a conventional military victory. Officials increasingly acknowledge that some Taliban fighters may eventually have to be reconciled with the Afghan government, provided they renounce al-Qaeda, stop fighting and accept the constitutional order.

The intended end state is an Afghan government able to control its territory with national soldiers and police, supported by political agreements that isolate hard-line insurgents. To reach that point, the United States and its allies are expanding and training Afghan security forces.

That effort has been hampered by illiteracy, desertion, corruption, ethnic imbalances and weak leadership. Afghan army units have improved in some areas, but many still depend on NATO forces for transportation, intelligence, air support and logistics. The police are widely regarded as less capable and more vulnerable to corruption.

The forthcoming Afghan election is therefore a key test. Western governments hope a credible vote will strengthen the legitimacy of President Hamid Karzai’s government or that of any successor. But allegations of fraud, insecurity and official corruption threaten to undermine the result.

American and British officials recognize that military gains will not endure without better governance. In many districts, the Taliban has exploited anger over corrupt police, abusive officials, unemployment and the slow delivery of basic services. Western strategy calls for civilian specialists and Afghan administrators to move into newly secured areas, but the civilian effort has often lagged behind military operations.

The sharp rise in deaths has also revived questions about how long the mission will last. Obama has ordered additional forces to Afghanistan while promising a broad review of progress. British officials similarly say their commitment is not open-ended, although neither government has set a near-term deadline for withdrawal.

Setting a fixed departure date, they argue, could encourage the Taliban to wait out the coalition and frighten Afghans who might otherwise cooperate with the government. At the same time, officials say continued support depends on measurable progress in Afghan governance, security-force development and the protection of civilians.

The political risk is substantial. As casualties mount, voters may become less willing to accept an operation whose objectives have shifted over the years—from destroying al-Qaeda and toppling the Taliban government to counterinsurgency, reconstruction and state-building.

For now, Washington and London maintain that the consequences of leaving would be greater than the costs of staying. Their case rests not on the promise of a quick victory but on the judgment that Afghanistan, if again abandoned to the Taliban and transnational militants, could pose a direct threat well beyond its borders.

The deadliest month of the war has therefore produced calls for better equipment, a clearer strategy and faster Afghan self-reliance—but not, from either government, a decision to leave.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a late-July 2009 CNN report using quotations from Hillary Clinton, David Miliband, and Richard Holbrooke about coalition strategy, moderate Taliban reintegration, Afghan elections, and public doubts about the war.
counterfactuals.output:
**Coalition weighs Taliban reintegration as doubts over Afghan war grow**  
*CNN — July 28, 2009*

LONDON (CNN) — Senior U.S. and British officials are calling for a broader political strategy in Afghanistan, arguing that military pressure must be combined with efforts to draw lower-level Taliban fighters away from the insurgency.

Secretary of State Hillary Clinton said Washington and Kabul were prepared to accept insurgents who abandon violence and break with al Qaeda.

“We and our Afghan allies stand ready to welcome anyone supporting the Taliban who renounces al Qaeda, lays down their arms and is willing to participate in the free and open society that is enshrined in the Afghan constitution,” Clinton said in a July foreign-policy address.

British Foreign Secretary David Miliband echoed that approach Monday, telling a NATO audience in Brussels that the coalition could not achieve its goals through force alone.

“There is no purely military route to victory in Afghanistan,” Miliband said. Although negotiating with people linked to attacks on coalition troops was difficult, he argued, the insurgency was not a single, unified movement and could be divided.

The proposed strategy distinguishes between hard-line Taliban leaders tied to al Qaeda and “reconcilable” fighters motivated by money, tribal rivalries, intimidation or dissatisfaction with the Afghan government. Officials describe the immediate goal as reintegration — persuading individuals and local commanders to stop fighting — rather than striking a settlement with the Taliban leadership.

Richard Holbrooke, the Obama administration’s special representative for Afghanistan and Pakistan, has said such an effort must be led by Afghans and supported by jobs, security and credible local government.

“Every insurgency ends with a political settlement,” Holbrooke said, while cautioning that outreach would not extend to al Qaeda or irreconcilable Taliban figures. Coalition officials, he added, must give rank-and-file fighters a viable alternative to the insurgency.

The debate comes as Afghanistan prepares for presidential and provincial elections on August 20. President Hamid Karzai is seeking another term, but insecurity, allegations of corruption and doubts about the government’s reach have raised concerns about turnout and the legitimacy of the result.

Clinton has described the elections as an important test, saying they must be “free, fair and secure.” Western officials, however, acknowledge that voting may be difficult or impossible in some Taliban-dominated districts.

The political push is unfolding alongside a major increase in U.S. forces and intensified combat in southern Afghanistan. President Obama ordered thousands of additional troops into the country this year, describing the region as central to the fight against al Qaeda.

But after nearly eight years of war, public support is weakening in both the United States and Britain. Rising casualties have prompted questions about the mission’s goals, its duration and whether Afghan institutions can eventually assume responsibility.

Clinton acknowledged those concerns, saying the public was “rightly concerned” about the course of the conflict. Administration officials say the answer is not an open-ended military campaign, but a coalition strategy that protects the population, strengthens Afghan security forces, supports credible elections and separates pragmatic insurgents from committed extremists.

Miliband said maintaining public backing would require governments to explain both the stakes and the limits of the mission.
